L0@P0: FedSight AI: Multi-Agent System Architecture for
L1@P0: Federal Funds Target Rate Prediction
L2@P0: Yuhan Hou∗ 1, Tianji Rao∗ 1,2, Jeremy Matthew Tan∗ 1, Adler Viton∗ 1,2, Xiyue Zhang∗ 1
L3@P0: David Ye1, Abhishek Kodi2, Sanjana Dulam2, Aditya Paul2, YiKai Feng2
L4@P0: 1Duke University, Durham, NC, USA
L5@P0: 2BNY AI Hub, New York, NY, USA
L6@P0: Abstract
L7@P0: The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) sets the federal funds rate, shaping
L8@P0: monetary policy and the broader economy. We introduce FedSight AI, a multiagent framework that uses large language models (LLMs) to simulate FOMC
L9@P0: deliberations and predict policy outcomes. Member agents analyze structured
L10@P0: indicators and unstructured inputs such as the Beige Book, debate options, and
L11@P0: vote, replicating committee reasoning. A Chain-of-Draft (CoD) extension further improves efficiency and accuracy by enforcing concise multistage reasoning.
L12@P0: Evaluated at 2023-2024 meetings, FedSight CoD achieved accuracy of 93.75%
L13@P0: and stability of 93.33%, outperforming baselines including MiniFed and Ordinal
L14@P0: Random Forest (RF), while offering transparent reasoning aligned with real FOMC
L15@P0: communications.
L16@P0: 1 Introduction
L17@P0: The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) sets the federal funds rate, and its decisions reflect
L18@P0: diverse philosophies and regional concerns. Traditional econometric models assume static relationships, while machine learning methods improve accuracy but remain opaque and cannot incorporate
L19@P0: unstructured inputs such as speeches or Beige Books, which strongly influence policy makers’ reasoning [1–3]. Leveraging LLMs, prior multi-agent work simulates FOMC-style deliberations [4].
L20@P0: Building on this, we present FedSight AI: agents jointly analyze structured indicators and unstructured
L21@P0: narratives, deliberate, vote, and produce forecasts with interpretable reasoning; a CoD mechanism
L22@P0: streamlines multi-stage reasoning [5]. Our contributions are threefold: (1) one of the first forecasting systems treating FOMC decisions as deliberative institutional outcomes rather than black-box
L23@P0: mappings; (2) integration of structured indicators and unstructured narratives in agent deliberations;
L24@P0: and (3) FedSight CoD: 93.75% accuracy and 93.33% stability on recent meetings—outperforming
L25@P0: MiniFed [4] and an Ordinal Random Forest [6]—with transparent, FOMC-aligned reasoning.
L26@P0: 2 Related Studies
L27@P0: Interest Rate Prediction. Forecasting interest rates has been widely studied through diverse
L28@P0: approaches. Classical econometric models, such as the expectations hypothesis [7] and the Taylor Rule
L29@P0: [8], provided interpretable but simplified frameworks. Later, time-series models including VARs and
L30@P0: DTSMs [9, 10] incorporated macroeconomic dynamics, while machine learning approaches—random
L31@P0: forests, boosting, deep neural networks, and LSTMs [3, 11]—captured nonlinear relationships and
L32@P0: sequential dependencies. More recently, an Ordinal Random Forest model [6] is proposed and
L33@P0: achieved strong predictive performance, offering a benchmark for our research. Yet these methods
L34@P0: remain limited by opacity and by their inability to reflect the deliberative nature of collective
L35@P0: policymaking, motivating alternative frameworks.
L36@P0: ∗Equal contribution. Authors listed alphabetically.
L37@P0: 39th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2025) Workshop: Generative AI in
L38@P0: Finance.
L39@P0-1: arXiv:2512.15728v1 [q-fin.GN] 5 Dec 2025Multi-Agent System Frameworks. Parallel to econometric and Machine Learning (ML) models,
L40@P1: advances in multi-agent systems (MAS) with LLMs emphasize autonomy, communication, and
L41@P1: collaboration [12]. In finance, FinCon demonstrated agent collaboration for portfolio management,
L42@P1: but with hierarchical constraints. More relevant is MiniFed [4], which simulates FOMC meetings
L43@P1: through five stages of agent discussion, persuasion, and voting, showing high predictive accuracy
L44@P1: and behavioral realism. Our framework builds on these developments but diverges structurally: each
L45@P1: agent represents an independent FOMC participant with unique interpretations, enabling a more
L46@P1: faithful simulation of policy deliberations and providing interpretable interest rate forecasts.
L47@P1: 3 Data and Methodology
L48@P1: 3.1 Data Description
L49@P1: Our target variable is the change in the Federal Funds Target Rate (FFTR) at each FOMC meeting,
L50@P1: expressed in basis points. Our dataset covers 16 scheduled meetings from February 2023 to December
L51@P1: 2024.
L52@P1: Structured Inputs. We compile structured predictors from six domains: inflation, monetary
L53@P1: indicators, economic activity and growth, political environment, past rate decisions, and market
L54@P1: expectations. These variables capture the standard economic signals considered in prior literature
L55@P1: and are aligned to values available two days before each meeting. The complete variable list and
L56@P1: definitions are provided in Appendix A.1 Table 2.
L57@P1: Unstructured Inputs. Beyond numerical indicators, we incorporate unstructured data that reflect
L58@P1: qualitative aspects of FOMC deliberations. First, the Beige Book2 provides anecdotal evidence from
L59@P1: all 12 Federal Reserve districts, covering labor markets, pricing pressures, and regional conditions.
L60@P1: Second, the Dot Plot3encodes each policymaker’s forward-looking expectations for the policy rate,
L61@P1: allowing us to capture consensus and disagreement. We also reference FedWatch market-implied
L62@P1: probabilities4. These sources, often overlooked in prior work, provide richer context for simulating
L63@P1: the reasoning processes of FOMC participants.
L64@P1: By combining structured and unstructured data, we aim to reflect both quantitative signals and the
L65@P1: qualitative narratives that shape policy decisions. Details of unstructured input preprocessing are
L66@P1: provided in the Appendix B.
L67@P1: 3.2 FedSight AI Multi-Agent System for FOMC Prediction
L68@P1: Unlike prior forecasting models that directly map economic indicators to policy outcomes, our
L69@P1: framework is designed to replicate the deliberative nature of the FOMC rate decisions. The central
L70@P1: motivation is that interest rate decisions are collective reasoning processes in which policymakers
L71@P1: weigh quantitative data, qualitative narratives, and peer perspectives. FedSight AI embeds this
L72@P1: institutional process into a multi-agent architecture, enabling prediction that is both accurate and
L73@P1: transparent.
L74@P1: Framework Design. FedSight AI is implemented in CrewAI as a structured sequence of tasks
L75@P1: carried out by heterogeneous agents (Figure 1). The system consists of an Analyst, an Economist,
L76@P1: and three Member agents. The Analyst interprets Fed Funds Futures to extract market-implied
L77@P1: hike or cut probabilities, providing an external benchmark. The Economist then formulates three
L78@P1: candidate policy options—typically dovish, neutral, and hawkish—each with a macro rationale. The
L79@P1: Member agents independently analyze both structured indicators (inflation, growth, labor markets,
L80@P1: expectations) and unstructured sources (Beige Book narratives, dot plots), deliberate on the proposed
L81@P1: options, and exchange perspectives. Through this collaborative process, they mimic the dynamics of
L82@P1: real FOMC discussions before casting a vote. The final output is a simulated FOMC statement that
L83@P1: consolidates the decision and its rationale.

L93@P2: Representative Agents. To ensure realism without excessive complexity, the Member agents are
L94@P2: derived from a clustering procedure applied to historical FOMC participants (Appendix A.2). This
L95@P2: yields three representative archetypes: Regional Pragmatists, Academic Balancers, and Central
L96@P2: Policymakers. Each archetype encodes a distinct economic orientation, capturing diverse viewpoints
L97@P2: while remaining tractable. This design balances computational efficiency with behavioral fidelity.
L98@P2: Key Contributions. This architecture advances beyond black-box forecasting approaches in three
L99@P2: ways. First, it integrates structured and unstructured data into a deliberative workflow, reflecting how
L100@P2: policymakers weigh both statistics and narratives. Second, it operationalizes collective reasoning and
L101@P2: dissent, producing not only point predictions but also interpretable reasoning chains aligned with
L102@P2: real-world policy communication. Third, the clustering-based design grounds the agents in realistic
L103@P2: archetypes, providing a principled way to capture heterogeneity without inflating system size. In this
L104@P2: sense, FedSight AI is among the first forecasting systems to treat FOMC decisions as the emergent
L105@P2: outcome of an institution rather than an isolated statistical mapping.
L106@P2: 3.3 Performance Metrics
L107@P2: We assess performance with six metrics spanning accuracy, consistency, interpretability, efficiency,
L108@P2: and error: Total Accuracy and Agent Accuracy quantify predictive accuracy; Voting Stability measures
L109@P2: consistency across runs; Semantic Similarity evaluates alignment of generated statements with official
L110@P2: communications; Average Tokens captures computational efficiency; and MAE summarizes residual
L111@P2: error. Together, these provide a comprehensive, multidimensional evaluation. The exact formulas are
L112@P2: provided in Appendix C.
L113@P2: 4 Experiments and Results
L114@P2: 4.1 Experiment Settings
L115@P2: We begin by establishing a baseline evaluation of FedSight AI and then introduce two extensions designed to enhance agent performance and efficiency: FedSight ICL and FedSight CoD. All variations
L116@P2: use OpenAI GPT 4o agents with robust instructions that define roles and tasks. Approximately 26
L117@P2: million tokens are used across all experiments and comparisons.
L118@P2: Backtesting Setup. FedSight AI is evaluated on all 16 FOMC meetings from 2023–2024 (9 holds,
L119@P2: 3 cuts, 4 hikes), a distribution consistent with the past two decades (Appendi D Table 4). Each
L120@P2: meeting is simulated five times to account for the stochasticity of LLM outputs. This backtesting
L121@P2: setup provides the foundation for assessing subsequent enhancements.
L122@P2: FedSight ICL. To strengthen agent reasoning before predicting future meetings, we applied a
L123@P2: simulation-based fine-tuning procedure inspired by in-context learning (ICL). Agents were placed in
L124@P2: the context of historical FOMC meetings (e.g., October 2019, January 2022, March 2022), asked to
L125@P2: vote on rate decisions, justify their reasoning, and forecast year-end targets. Subsequently, the true
L126@P2: decisions were revealed, and agents reflected on reasoning gaps and adjusted their strategies. These
L127@P2: iterative simulations were stored as long-term memory, enabling agents to recall lessons in later tasks.
L128@P2: This extension refines the baseline system by embedding empirical feedback in memory.
L129@P2: FedSight CoD. Complementing FedSight ICL, we also incorporated the CoD framework [5, 13],
L130@P2: which extends Chain-of-Thought prompting by enforcing concise multi-stage reasoning. Specifically,
L131@P2: prompts required agents to produce minimal-step drafts (≤30 words per step), followed by revisions.
L132@P2: This reduced token counts and computational costs while preserving critical reasoning content. Prior
L133@P2: work shows that CoD enhances coherence and factual accuracy, and our adaptation confirms its utility
L134@P2: in balancing interpretability with efficiency in multi-agent deliberations.
L135@P2-3: 34.2 Results
L136@P3: Table 1 reports performance across six metrics. For additional context, we include a simple Linear
L137@P3: Regression (LR) baseline trained on all quantitative predictors and binary indicators. FedSight
L138@P3: CoD consistently outperforms both the baseline FedSight AI and FedSight ICL, achieving the
L139@P3: highest accuracy (93.75%), agent agreement (90.22%), and stability (93.33%) while also reducing
L140@P3: computational cost (60k tokens on average). The only dimension where the baseline marginally leads
L141@P3: is statement similarity, though differences are small (∼1–2%). Overall, FedSight CoD provides the
L142@P3: best balance between accuracy, interpretability, and efficiency.
